paper.title_en: On the Capacity of Erasure-Prone Quantum Storage With Erasure-Prone Entanglement Assistance
paper.abstract_en: A quantum message is encoded into <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> quantum storage systems <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$Q_{1} {\dots } Q_{N}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> with assistance from <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> maximally entangled bi-partite quantum systems <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$A_{1}B_{1}, {\dots }, A_{N_{B}}B_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, that are prepared in advance such that <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$B_{1} {\dots } B_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> are stored separately as entanglement assistance (EA) systems, while <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$A_{1} {\dots } A_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> are made available to the encoder. Both the storage systems and EA systems are erasure-prone. The quantum message must be recoverable given any <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K$ </tex-math></inline-formula> of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> storage systems along with any <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> EA systems. The capacity for this setting is the maximum size of the quantum message, given that the size of each EA system is <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>. All system sizes are relative to the size of a storage system, which is normalized to unity. The exact capacity is characterized as a function of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N,K,N_{B},K_{B}, \lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> in all cases, with one exception. The capacity remains open for an intermediate range of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> values when a strict majority of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> storage systems, and a strict non-zero minority of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> EA systems, are erased. For the open regime, we conjecture that our inner (achievability) bound is tight. As a key stepping stone, an analogous classical storage (with shared-randomness assistance) problem is introduced. A set of constraints is identified for the classical problem, including that the classical storage systems can recover the shared-randomness in particular, such that classical linear code constructions translate to quantum storage codes, and the converse bounds for the two settings utilize similar insights. In particular, the capacity characterizations for the classical and quantum settings are shown to be identical in all cases where the capacity is settled.
